topic: Close-up A1+ · Unit 2: Friends & Fun — Reading · SB 18, 19 · WB 10 (HW) · Grade 6 (periods 4–5)
title: After-School Club Academy
subtitle: Invite them properly, or they will never come 🎟️

features.title: Read for the Answer
features.desc: Four friends, four timetables — find who is free, on which day, and where.

features.title: Invite, Accept, Refuse
features.desc: The three moves of a polite exchange, drilled until they come out by themselves.

features.title: Fill the Gaps
features.desc: Complete two real conversations — predict the missing language, then check it.

features.title: Four Games
features.desc: Match the people, scramble the words, pair the replies, sort the phrases.

method.phase: Vocab → Reading → Game → Review (periods 4–5 of the unit-2 session)

games.name: People & Information
games.why: reading against a text — the reader must hold one person's line and search the whole text for the matching detail

games.name: Word Scramble
games.why: retrieval under a clock — the hint is the meaning, so the word comes back out of memory, not off the page

games.name: Invite & Reply
games.why: functional pairing — an invitation and its answer are learned as ONE exchange, which is how a conversation is produced

games.name: Invite, Accept or Refuse
games.why: metacognitive sorting — the learner must name what the speaker is DOING with the words, which is the functional-language skill itself

voice: Loud and wrong beats silent and correct. Every single time.
You are not teaching English. You are building Tigers.

storyline: Mai invites Nam to the chess club and Nam says no first, with a reason, then yes to a better day. The group chat shows four friends failing to find a free afternoon. The reading text is their four timetables, and the lesson ends with an invitation the learner writes himself.

rooms.title: The Entrance
rooms.label: Warm-Up
rooms.content:
Two periods, four games, one invitation you write yourself 🎟️ Period 4 is the reading; period 5 is the speaking. By the end you can invite a friend, accept properly, and refuse without losing the friend.

  • Nine words: the days of the week, hobbies, clubs, practice — and the phrases that invite and answer
  • Four friends, four timetables, and how to match a person to the right information
  • How to say no politely — with a reason, not just “no”
  • You will invite a partner to something real, out loud

rooms.title: The Invitation
rooms.label: Scene
rooms.content:
Mai: Nam, would you like to join the chess club? We meet on Tuesday and Thursday 🎟️
Nam: Tuesday is impossible for me — I have swimming practice.
Mai: What about Thursday, then?
Nam: Thursday is fine! I'd love to.
Mai: Good. How often do you practise swimming?
Nam: Three times a week. My dad says I am never at home 😄
🤔 Reality check: Nam says no first, then yes — and he gives a reason for both. A refusal with a reason is not a rejection; it is information. That is how you keep the friend and still get your Thursday.

rooms.title: The Group Chat
rooms.label: Text Scene
rooms.content:
Linh: guys, after-school club sign-up is today 🙄
Tuan: do you fancy the science club? Tuesday, Room 8 😏
Linh: Tuesday I have guitar. How about Thursday?
Tuan: Thursday I'm at art club. Maybe next time 🎨
Linh: Friday I sing in the choir. We are all busy. That is why we plan first!
🤔 Reality check: nobody in this chat says the word “no”. They say I have… + a day. Giving your reason is what makes a refusal sound friendly instead of rude.
Pro Tip: the three moves of a polite exchange — invite (“Would you like to…?” / “Do you fancy…?” / “How about…?”), accept (“I'd love to!” / “That sounds great.”), refuse politely (“Sorry, I can't — I have…” / “Maybe next time.”). A refusal without a reason sounds cold; a refusal with a reason sounds like a friend.

rooms.title: The Words
rooms.label: Learn
rooms.content:
1. the days of the week: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday — the club meets on Tuesday and Thursday.
2. hobby: something you enjoy doing in your free time — chess, swimming, singing.
3. after-school activity: something you do when lessons finish — a club, a class, a practice.
4. club: a group that meets to do one activity together — a chess club, a science club.
5. practice: the time you spend training at a sport or a skill — swimming practice, football practice.
6. Would you like to…? the polite way to invite someone. Would you like to join the club?
7. I'd love to! saying yes to an invitation — and it sounds happy, not flat.
8. Sorry, I can't — I have… saying no politely, and giving your reason. Sorry, I can't — I have guitar.
9. How often…? the question that asks about a routine. How often do you practise? — Three times a week.
The move to keep: a bare “no” sounds cold. Sorry, I can't — I have football practice. says the same thing and keeps the friend.

rooms.title: Four Friends, Four Clubs
rooms.label: Reading
rooms.content:
Mai likes quiet games. She goes to the chess club on Tuesday and Thursday in Room 12. She is free on Monday and Friday.

Nam is sporty. He has swimming practice on Wednesday after school and he plays football at the weekend. Practice finishes at six.

Linh is musical. She has a guitar lesson on Monday and she sings in the school choir on Friday.

Tuan joins everything. On Tuesday he goes to the science club and on Thursday he has the art club. He says those are his favourite days of the week.

Reading move 1 — matching people and information: read the question first (which day? which club?), then find the person, then find the information next to that name. The answer is where the two meet — never guess from the first name you see.
Reading move 2 — predicting missing language: in a gap in a conversation, read the words before the gap. A question with “Would you like…?” can only be answered with an accept or a refuse — that is your prediction. Then check it against the words after the gap.
🤔 Reality check: Mai, Nam, Linh and Tuan are all busy on different days. Anyone who wants to start a new club has to read the whole text before choosing a day — that is what “matching people and information” really tests.

rooms.title: Complete the Conversation
rooms.label: Gaps
rooms.content:
How to do this room: do not read the gap first — read the line after it. The reply tells you what kind of line the gap has to be. Predict, then choose.
Complete the conversation: _____ join the chess club? We meet on Tuesday and Thursday.
— I'd love to, but I can't on Tuesday — I have swimming practice.
Complete the conversation: Do you fancy the science club on Tuesday?
— _____ I have guitar on Tuesday. How about Thursday?
Complete the conversation: How often do you practise swimming?
— _____.
🤔 Reality check: you did not need a grammar rule for any of these — you needed the line after the gap. In a real conversation, the reply is your best clue about what to say next.

rooms.title: Game 1 — People & Information
rooms.label: Game 1
rooms.content: How to win: click a name on the left, then the information that belongs to that person on the right. Six pairs — every answer is in the text you just read, so read slowly and match the whole line.

rooms.title: Game 2 — Word Scramble
rooms.label: Game 2
rooms.content: How to win: the hint under each row is the meaning — read it, then click the tiles in order. A wrong word shakes and clears itself, so nothing is lost.

rooms.title: Game 3 — Invite & Reply
rooms.label: Game 3
rooms.content: How to win: click an invitation on the left, then the reply that answers it on the right. Six pairs — three accept and three refuse politely. Wrong pairs shake and let go.

rooms.title: Game 4 — Invite, Accept or Refuse?
rooms.label: Game 4
rooms.content:
How to win: click a phrase, then the group it belongs to. Ask yourself one question — what is this person doing with these words: asking, agreeing, or saying no nicely?

The three groups: INVITING = you are asking someone to do something · ACCEPTING = you are saying yes, happily · REFUSING = you are saying no, with a reason.

rooms.title: The Test
rooms.label: Test
rooms.content:
Scenario: You want your friend to come to the chess club with you. Which sentence is a real invitation?
Scenario: Your friend invites you to the art club on Thursday. You play football on Thursday. What do you say?
Scenario: A new club meets on Friday after school. Which friend already has something on that day?

rooms.title: The Key
rooms.label: Mastery
rooms.content:
🎓 You now hold the key
  • Invite: Would you like to…? · Do you fancy…? · How about…? · Let's…
  • Accept happily: I'd love to! · That sounds great. · Count me in.
  • Refuse politely: Sorry, I can't — I have… · Maybe next time. Always give the reason.
  • Words: the days of the week · hobby · after-school activity · club · practice · How often…?
  • Match people and information: read the question, find the person, find the information next to that name — the answer is where the two meet.
  • Predict the gap: the words before a gap tell you what kind of reply fits, and the words after it confirm your prediction.
Level Up: invite a partner to a real after-school activity, out loud — by name, with a day and a time. They refuse politely with a reason, and you offer a second day. Then swap.
Challenge: write three short sentences to summarise the four friends' text, then write two extra comprehension questions for a partner — with the answers underlined in the text.
🤔 Reality check: the value in this lesson is including others. A polite refusal is not a closed door — it is a friend telling you the truth about their week, and it usually comes with another day.
Write it down (WB page 10): write your own invitation — a name, an activity and a day — and then the polite refusal you would give if you were busy.
